# Environment update
 - Primary working directory: /Users/darshpoddar/Coding/craigslist/demo (was /Users/darshpoddar/Coding)

I'd reuse the setup from your Craigslist scam video and add your on-camera footage to it. That earlier video was built from a written script, a voiceover recorded separately, and a screen recording run by a script in `craigslist/demo/record.mjs` and timed to the voiceover. It took 13 attempts, but every attempt could be redone exactly, which is why it came out polished.

**Suggested structure (60–90s):**

| Time | Shot | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 0–10s | You on camera (C014-style front shot) | The problem: "Most signups are a Gmail address and nothing else. You have no idea who they are." |
| 10–55s | Screen recording, your voice over it | One signup arrives → Autumn resolves it to a person, company and role → enriches it → it lands in Slack or the CRM. Zoom in on each key moment. |
| 55–75s | Back to you, with cuts to the side angle (C017-style) | Why it matters: which signups to follow up first, response speed, a real result from your `signup-id` campaign. |
| 75–80s | End card | Logo and call to action. |

**Order of work:**
1. **Write the script first,** one row per moment with its timing, like `narration-take9.md`. Everything else follows from it.
2. **Record the voice and on-camera parts.** If you film more on-camera bits, use the same glass-wall set and two camera angles. Cutting between the front and side shots hides any edits to your speech.
3. **Record the screen as a script, not by hand.** Adapt `record.mjs`, which already has the smooth fake cursor, 1080p/4K capture and timing to the voiceover. Use a test signup or one you have permission to show. A real person's details shouldn't be in a public video.
4. **Finish the video:** captions (most people watch muted), name and title captions under you on camera, quiet music, and audio levelled to −16 LUFS like last time. You were unsure how the audio sounded, so we'll measure it rather than rely on how it sounds through speakers.

**Your existing footage:** I can't tell yet whether C004, C011 or C014 actually talk about signup deanonymization. There's no transcription tool installed. I can install Whisper, transcribe all the takes, and tell you which lines could go in this video. That decides whether you need to film again.

To write the first script draft, I need two things from you:
- **Who is it for, and where will it be shown?** For example, possible customers on your landing page, a LinkedIn post, or investors.
- **Which product screens do you want to show?** Is there a running version of the signup tool I can record from?

How Vercel runs technical support on Plain (65% less ticket volume) | Plain | 120 s
David Totten, VP of Field Engineering at Vercel, explains why Vercel moved its technical support team to Plain instead of building its own support stack, and what changed after the move.

Since moving to Plain:
• Each support engineer closes 38% more tickets a week
• First response time is down 79%
• Customer wait time is down by close to 50%
• The Case Retro Agent, which Vercel built and connected to Plain, saves 65% of ticket volume

Read the case study: plain.com/customers/vercel

Chapters:
• 0:00 Customers need information quickly
• 0:22 Why Vercel chose Plain
• 0:40 Results
• 1:03 The Case Retro Agent
• 1:28 Plain across the business
• 1:42 Support and revenue

Plain is how the world's most beloved software companies work with their customers. Learn more at www.plain.com.

content.content:
# sixtyfive

Autumn internal operations: outreach, analytics, Slack notifications, lifecycle email,
and evaluation tooling. Orchard remains a separate repository. The Autumn product
is also separate; this repository reads its data through adapters.

[outreach/](outreach/README.md) contains the consolidated LinkedIn campaign code and
Post Studio. [Operations layout](docs/OPERATIONS.md) explains source ownership,
independent deployments, and the boundaries for future CRM work.

Activepieces monitoring runs on the VPS. The Carta watchdog uses a local Python
runner and systemd timer; [setup and migration](activepieces/monitor/README.md)
preserve existing incident state when retiring the old Modal monitor.

```
src/slack/           Slack
src/email/           lifecycle email (welcome, nudges, suppression)
src/arena/           agent arena: suites, benchmarks, runs, judging, elo, grading, lineage
src/autoresearch/    lineage records + diagnosis for arena experiments
src/beanstalk/       vendored from Autumn: tier slot config
src/router/          arena / lineage / autoresearch HTTP API
src/autumn.py        read-only Autumn adapters
src/aws.py           DynamoDB + S3
app.py               Modal app
grafana/             source of truth for Grafana Cloud dashboards + alert rules (see grafana/README.md)
```

## Grafana

Dashboards and alert rules for the `beanstalk` Grafana Cloud stack live in `grafana/` and deploy
via CI: PRs touching `grafana/**` are validated, merges to `main` push to Grafana (pruning
dashboards removed from git) using the `GRAFANA_EDITOR_TOKEN` secret; `GRAFANA_SLACK_WEBHOOK`
additionally wires all `service=autumn` alerts to #grafana-alerts. Details in `grafana/README.md`.

## Daily KPI digest

`kpi_digest` (`app_observability.py`, its own Modal app `observability`, 7:50 PT) posts yesterday's KPIs to `SLACK_PRODUCT_CHANNEL`
(default #grafana-alerts): tasks, cost p50/p90 (exact per-run credits), run-duration p50/p90,
LLM latency, and cache-hit rate split by tier (Ranger/Scout), plus max concurrent tasks, TTFT
and turn-time percentiles, and error counts. Tier task counts come from
`beanstalk-tasks.runtime_tier`; everything else is queried from Grafana Cloud Prometheus via
the datasource proxy, so the `slack` Modal secret needs `GRAFANA_SERVICE_TOKEN` (read-only,
datasources:query) and optionally `SLACK_PRODUCT_CHANNEL`. Metrics grouped by the `tier`
label fall back to model→tier mapping (tiers.yaml) until the autumn instrumentation deploy.
Manual run: `modal run app.py::kpi_digest --force`.

`health_probe` (`app_observability.py`, every minute) is the external uptime check. It probes every
public surface concurrently: the API (`/health/info` deps, `/health` response time, `/openapi.json`),
staging, `platform.autumn.ai`, the marketing site, the docs, and the seven Modal services. Probing
`/health/info` is also what makes Autumn run its dependency probes, which feed
`autumn_dep_failures_total` and the `autumn-dep-degraded` alert.

On failure it posts to `SLACK_PRODUCT_CHANNEL` with a per-target failure streak and a 30 minute
cooldown, opens a Grafana annotation that widens into a band on recovery, and fires an incident.io
alert keyed on the target. Every run pushes one sample per target to Grafana Cloud, which is what the
`autumn-uptime` dashboard reads. See `grafana/README.md` for the four Grafana credentials and
`src/metrics.py` for the declared metric surface.

The `grafana` Modal secret needs `GRAFANA_PROM_WRITE_TOKEN` (a Cloud access policy token with
`metrics:write`) and `GRAFANA_ANNOTATION_TOKEN` (an Editor service-account token) for those last two.

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Read

Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

'update': upload to a specific guide by short_code. 'create': always make a new link. 'delete': remove the guide named by short_code; with no short_code, nothing is deleted and the user's guides are listed.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. The cache is positional: agent() calls replay from cache up to the first call that failed, no longer matches the earlier run (edited, added, removed or reordered) or never started in it; that call and every call after it run again, even when their own (prompt, opts) are unchanged. A call a usage limit refused, or one still running when the run stopped, usually runs again without ending reuse: finished calls after it still come from cache. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

Searches for messages, files in ALL Slack channels, including public channels, private channels, DMs, and group DMs. Current logged in user's user_id is U0BE37UJKJB.

---
`query` should include keywords or natural language question with search modifiers.

Search modifiers:
  in:channel-name / in:<#C123456> / -in:channel   Channel filter
  in:<@U123456> / in:@username                     DM filter
  from:<@U123456> / from:username                  Author filter (angle brackets are literal for IDs)
  to:<@U123456> / to:me                            Recipient filter
  creator:@user                                    Canvas creator filter
  is:thread / is:saved / has:pin / has:link / has:file  Content filters
  has::emoji: / hasmy::emoji:                      Reaction filters
  before:YYYY-MM-DD / after:YYYY-MM-DD / on:YYYY-MM-DD / during:month  Date filters
  "exact phrase" / -word / * (wildcard, min 3 chars)  Text matching

File search: use `content_types="files"` with `type:` filter (images, documents, pdfs, spreadsheets, presentations, canvases, lists, emails, audio, videos). All standard modifiers work with file searches.

Search types:
1. Natural language —  ❌ Semantic search is not available for this user.
2. Keyword — exact matches, space-separated = AND, no boolean operators (AND/OR/NOT).

Use slack_read_thread for thread details, slack_read_canvas for canvas content, slack_read_channel for surrounding messages.

Strategy: break into multiple small searches, use modifiers to narrow, try keyword then semantic (or vice versa), broaden if 0 results.

---

Examples:
  ✅ Use (with user consent)
    query="What's our holiday schedule? in:#general"
    query="bug report after:2024-01-08" sort="timestamp"
    query="from:<@U123456> in:dev bug report"

Additional parameters:
  include_context (Optional[bool])  Include surrounding context messages for each result (default: true). Ignored when response_format is 'concise', which never shows context. Set to false to reduce response size.
  max_context_length (Optional[int])  Max character length for each context message. Longer messages are truncated.

channel_types.description: Comma-separated list of channel types to include in the search. Defaults to 'public_channel,private_channel,mpim,im' (all channel types including private channels, group DMs, and DMs). limit.description: Number of results to return, up to a max of 20. Defaults to 20.

after.description: Only messages after this Unix timestamp (inclusive)

before.description: Only messages before this Unix timestamp (inclusive)

content.content:
# Autumn Design Guidelines

Rules for building Autumn UI — landing, product, anything new. Follow every rule unless a more specific rule overrides it. Tokens live in `styles/tokens.css`; components in `components/`. Import components before writing new ones; never re-hardcode a value that has a token.

**The look in one line:** warm kraft paper, espresso ink, one burnt-orange accent, mono-caps micro-labels, dithered pixels, physical micro-interactions. Earthy and editorial — never neon, never glassy, never gray.

## Brand

- Use exactly one accent: `#d86b23` (`autumn-orange`). Never introduce a second decorative hue.
- Keep every neutral warm (hue 20–40°). Never `slate`, `zinc`, `gray-*`, pure `#fff`, or pure black.
- Tint shadows warm brown (`rgba(33,19,14,…)`). Never neutral-black shadows on light surfaces.
- Set micro-labels in mono caps: `font-mono uppercase text-[10–11px] tracking-[0.08–0.16em]`. This is the #1 signature — eyebrows, marketing buttons, table heads, badges, tool labels.
- Keep display type light: `font-normal`/`font-medium`, hero at weight 360, negative tracking. Never bold headings.
- Texture with Perlin/Bayer dithers, not blobs, glows, or glassmorphism.
- Show the real platform between hero and footer on marketing pages — actual product components rendering real-shaped data — or show nothing. Never fake browser mockups, invented screenshots, or lorem demos.

## Color

Contexts: `:root` product light (near-white) · `.dark` product dark (warm charcoal) · `.theme-canvas` kraft cream `#eee9e2` (landing, auth).

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `autumn-orange` | `#d86b23` | the accent: dots, live markers, `lead` badges, focus rings, selection |
| `ink` / `ink-hover` | `#21130e` / `#1a0f07` | dark fills, dark sections / hover when fills hollow out |
| `paper` / `paper-raised` | `#fffdfb` / `#fbfaf8` | card faces / raised band behind card clusters |
| `canvas` | `#eee9e2` | kraft page background |
| `card-border` / `card-border-b` | `#c8bfb4` / `#b9aea2` | the emboss border pair |
| `eyebrow` | `#b5601f` | eyebrow label text |
| `tan` / `tan-soft` | `#9f6b43` / `#c49368` | source counts, graph nodes |
| `well-1..4` | `#faf7f3 #f8f5f1 #f5f1ec #f3eee8` | chips → table heads → wells → card headers |
| `surface-1..3` | warm hsl ladder | sidebar, hovers, product elevation |

- Build text hierarchy with opacity, not separate grays: `text-foreground/60` body, `/72` prose, `/75` cells; on dark bands `text-background/90 → /42`.
- Elevate with the warmth ladder (`well-*`, `surface-*`), not shadows.
- Use semantic status color only in badges/status: positive `#4f9d69`-family, negative `#c2564b`-family. Never rely on color alone; pair with a text label.
- Prose links: `#2e6da4` (dark mode `#7a9ec4`).
- Set `color-scheme` per theme (tokens.css does this).

## Typography

- Sans: Geist. Mono: Geist Mono. Load via `next/font` with `--font-geist`/`--font-geist-mono`; system stacks are the fallback.
- Hero H1: `text-[clamp(2.25rem,5.4vw,3.9rem)] leading-[0.95] tracking-[-0.03em]`, weight 360.
- Section H2: `text-[clamp(1.8rem,3.6vw,2.6rem)] font-normal leading-[1.06] tracking-[-0.025em]`.
- Row H3: `text-[clamp(1.5rem,3vw,2.1rem)] font-normal leading-[1.08] tracking-[-0.02em]`.
- Marketing body: `text-[14.5px] leading-relaxed text-foreground/60`, max-w-md per column.
- Product ramp: 10.5 / 11 / 11.5 / 12 / 12.5 / 13 / 14px. Arbitrary values are expected.
- Emphasize with `font-medium` or `underline decoration-border decoration-2 underline-offset-4` on one word. Never bold, never italic.
- Use `tabular-nums` wherever digits line up: counts, timers, table columns.
- Use curly quotes (“ ”) and the ellipsis character (…), never three periods.
- Keep units and values together with ` `: `847 rows`.

## Layout

- Marketing container: `max-w-6xl px-6 md:px-10`; sections `py-20 md:py-28`; `.section-line` between bands.
- Canonical marketing page: cream canvas + dither hero → sunset transition → espresso `DarkBand` → footer CTA. Lean by default.
- Product shell: `h-screen overflow-hidden`, `w-64` sidebar `bg-surface-1 border-r border-foreground/10`, dense content, resizable panes.
- Full-bleed escape: `relative left-1/2 w-screen -translate-x-1/2`.
- Z ladder: dither 0 → content 10–49 → floating 999 → nav 1000 (marketing); overlays `z-50` (product).
- Align every element to something intentionally; adjust ±1px when perception beats geometry.
- Prefer flex/grid and `gap` over per-element margins; never measure in JS what CSS can lay out.
- Only render useful scrollbars; thin (4px) or hidden, warm-tinted.
- Verify layouts handle short, average, and very long content; verify mobile, laptop, ultra-wide.

## Design

- Cards are the emboss: `rounded-md border border-b-[1.5px] border-card-border border-b-card-border-b bg-paper`. Use `Card` — don't retype it.
- Hairlines everywhere: `border-border/40..70` dividers; `border-dashed border-border/55` menu separators.
- Tactile bottom edges are the only heavy borders: 1.5px card lip, `border-b-2 border-b-input` dropdown content, 3px auth card.
- Radius scale: `sm 4px · md 6px · lg 8px · xl 12px`; chips `rounded-[5px]`, markers `rounded-[2px]/[3px]`. Child radius ≤ parent radius, concentric. Nothing pill-shaped except dots and scroll thumbs.
- Shadows are tokens, two layers, warm: `shadow-card` (raise) · `shadow-float` (floating) · `shadow-dropdown` (menus) · `shadow-frame` (hero-scale). Never default Tailwind `shadow-lg`+.
- Allowed gradients, complete list: sunset transition (`SunsetTransition`), featured-panel `linear-gradient(180deg,#e8b465,#d86b23 38%,#3a2317 72%,#140d09)`, radial `Backlight` behind headings, dropdown orange glow `radial-gradient(165% 155% at 0% 120%, rgba(216,107,35,0.18), transparent 74%)`, skeleton shimmer, underline reveals. No others. No conic, no mesh, no gradient text.
- Icons: lucide only, stroke 1.5–2.1, 12–16px. No emoji in UI.

## Motion

- Ease entrances with `cubic-bezier(0.16,1,0.3,1)` (expo-out); plain `ease` for hovers.
- Durations: press 0.08–0.1s · hover 0.15–0.25s · UI enter 0.12–0.18s · scroll reveals 0.6–0.8s. Never > 1s.
- Animate only `transform` and `opacity`; prefer CSS over JS.
- Never `transition: all`. List properties explicitly (`.btn-press` shows the pattern).
- Animate in response to user action; avoid autoplay. Ambient loops (`dash-animate`, `node-glow`, dither) are the sanctioned exceptions.

"""Build src/captions.json: caption chunks on the output timeline from whisper word timings."""
import json, re, sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
edl = json.loads((ROOT / "src/edl.json").read_text())
FPS = edl["fps"]
FIX = {"autumn": "Autumn", "autumn's": "Autumn's", "gmail": "Gmail", "github": "GitHub", "github,": "GitHub,",
       "ex": "X", "ex,": "X,", "slack": "Slack", "ups": "up", "linkedin": "LinkedIn", "cto": "CTO"}

def words(take):
    d = json.loads((ROOT / f"scripts/transcripts/{take}.json").read_text())
    for s in d["transcription"]:
        w = s["text"].strip()
        if w:
            yield w, s["offsets"]["from"] / 1000, s["offsets"]["to"] / 1000

chunks, start = [], 0
for seg in edl["segments"]:
    n = round((seg["out"] - seg["in"]) * FPS)
    ws = [(FIX.get(w.lower(), w), a, b) for w, a, b in words(seg["take"]) if a >= seg["in"] - 0.05 and a < seg["in"] + n / FPS - 0.1]
    if ws and ws[0][0][0].islower():
        ws[0] = (ws[0][0][0].upper() + ws[0][0][1:], *ws[0][1:])
    cur = []
    for i, (w, a, b) in enumerate(ws):
        cur.append((w, a, b))
        nxt = ws[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(ws) else None
        brk = (nxt is None or re.search(r"[.,?!]$", w) and len(cur) >= 2 or len(cur) >= 5

"""Forced-align scripts/script.json to each EDL segment (torchaudio MMS_FA) -> scripts/words.json.
Run with a python that has torch/torchaudio: ~/.venvs/enhance/bin/python scripts/align.py"""
import json, re, subprocess
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np, torch, torchaudio

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
SRC = {"C011": "A001_11181800_C011.mov", "C017": "A001_11181814_C017.mov"}
edl = json.loads((ROOT / "src/edl.json").read_text())
texts = json.loads((ROOT / "scripts/script.json").read_text())
bundle = torchaudio.pipelines.MMS_FA
model, tok, aligner = bundle.get_model(with_star=False), bundle.get_tokenizer(), bundle.get_aligner()
SR = bundle.sample_rate
NUM = {"10": "ten"}

def norm(w):
    w = NUM.get(w.strip(",.?!"), w).lower().replace("-", "")
    w = {"x": "ex", "x,": "ex"}.get(w, w)
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z']", "", w)

out = []
for seg, text in zip(edl["segments"], texts):
    n = round((seg["out"] - seg["in"]) * edl["fps"]); dur = n / edl["fps"]
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-ss", str(seg["in"]), "-t", str(dur), "-i",
                          str(Path.home() / "Downloads" / SRC[seg["take"]]), "-map", "0:a:0", "-ac", "1", "-ar", str(SR),
                          "-f", "f32le", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    wav = torch.from_numpy(np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.float32).copy())[None]
    shown = text.split()
    words = [norm(w) for w in shown]
    with torch.inference_mode():
        em, _ = model(wav)
    spans = aligner(em[0], tok(words))
    ratio = wav.size(1) / em.size(1) / SR
    out.append([{"w": s, "a": round(sp[0].start * ratio, 3), "b": round(sp[-1].end * ratio, 3)} for s, sp in zip(shown, spans)])
    print(seg["take"], " ".join(f"{d['w']}@{d['a']:.2f}" for d in out[-1]))
(ROOT / "scripts/words.json").write_text(json.dumps(out, indent=0))

Run with a python that has torch/torchaudio: ~/.venvs/enhance/bin/python scripts/align.py"""
import json, re, subprocess
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np, torch, torchaudio

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
SRC = {"C011": "A001_11181800_C011.mov", "C017": "A001_11181814_C017.mov"}
edl = json.loads((ROOT / "src/edl.json").read_text())
texts = json.loads((ROOT / "scripts/script.json").read_text())
bundle = torchaudio.pipelines.MMS_FA
model, tok, aligner = bundle.get_model(with_star=False), bundle.get_tokenizer(), bundle.get_aligner()
SR = bundle.sample_rate
NUM = {"10": "ten"}

def norm(w):
    w = NUM.get(w.strip(",.?!"), w).lower().replace("-", "")
    w = {"x": "ex", "x,": "ex"}.get(w, w)
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z']", "", w)

out = []
for seg, text in zip(edl["segments"], texts):
    n = round((seg["out"] - seg["in"]) * edl["fps"]); dur = n / edl["fps"]
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-ss", str(seg["in"]), "-t", str(dur), "-i",
                          str(Path.home() / "Downloads" / SRC[seg["take"]]), "-map", "0:a:0", "-ac", "1", "-ar", str(SR),
                          "-f", "f32le", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    wav = torch.from_numpy(np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.float32).copy())[None]
    shown = text.split()
    words = [norm(w) for w in shown]
    with torch.inference_mode():
        em, _ = model(wav)
    spans = aligner(em[0], tok(words))
    ratio = wav.size(1) / em.size(1) / SR
    out.append([{"w": s, "a": round(sp[0].start * ratio, 3), "b": round(sp[-1].end * ratio, 3)} for s, sp in zip(shown, spans)])
    print(seg["take"], " ".join(f"{d['w']}@{d['a']:.2f}" for d in out[-1]))
(ROOT / "scripts/words.json").write_text(json.dumps(out, indent=0))
EOF

"""Cut the EDL segments from the voice takes and master them -> public/voice.wav.
AUDIO=raw uses the camera audio instead of the resemble-enhance output."""
import json, os, subprocess
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
edl = json.loads((ROOT / "src/edl.json").read_text())
kind = os.environ.get("AUDIO", "enhanced")
fps, fade = edl["fps"], 0.012
inputs, parts = [], []
for i, s in enumerate(edl["segments"]):
    dur = round((s["out"] - s["in"]) * fps) / fps
    inputs += ["-i", str(ROOT / f"audio/{s['take']}-{kind}.wav")]
    parts.append(f"[{i}:a]atrim={s['in']}:{s['in'] + dur},asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS,"
                 f"afade=t=in:d={fade},afade=t=out:st={dur - fade}:d={fade}[s{i}]")
n = len(edl["segments"])
chain = ("".join(f"[s{i}]" for i in range(n)) + f"concat=n={n}:v=0:a=1,"
         "highpass=f=75,equalizer=f=250:t=q:w=1.2:g=-2,equalizer=f=3500:t=q:w=1.5:g=1.5,"
         "acompressor=threshold=-22dB:ratio=2.5:attack=8:release=120:makeup=2,"
         f"apad=pad_dur={edl['endCardSeconds']},"

import json, re
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent

chunks, start = [], 0

    groups, cur = [], []
    for i, w in enumerate(ws):
        cur.append(w)
        left = len(ws) - i - 1
        if (re.search(r"[.,?!]$", w["w"]) and len(cur) >= 2) or len(cur) >= MAX and left != 1 or left == 0:

"""Bayer-dithered orange texture (brand: 'dithered pixels, not blobs') -> public/dither-*.png"""
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
from pathlib import Path
OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "public"
B = np.array([[0,32,8,40,2,34,10,42],[48,16,56,24,50,18,58,26],[12,44,4,36,14,46,6,38],[60,28,52,20,62,30,54,22],
              [3,35,11,43,1,33,9,41],[51,19,59,27,49,17,57,25],[15,47,7,39,13,45,5,37],[63,31,55,23,61,29,53,21]]) / 64
def make(name, field, px=6, rgb=(216,107,35), alpha=255):
    h, w = field.shape
    t = np.tile(B, (h // 8 + 1, w // 8 + 1))[:h, :w]
    on = field > t
    img = np.zeros((h, w, 4), np.uint8); img[on] = (*rgb, alpha)
    Image.fromarray(img).resize((w * px, h * px), Image.NEAREST).save(OUT / name)
W, H = 1920 // 6, 1080 // 6
y, x = np.mgrid[0:H, 0:W] / [H, W][0], np.mgrid[0:H, 0:W][1] / W
# end card: a sunrise of pixels rising from the bottom edge
make("dither-bottom.png", np.clip((y - 0.45) / 0.55, 0, 1) ** 1.6 * (0.75 + 0.25 * np.sin(x * 9 + 1.3)))
# cutaway backdrop: faint corners
r = np.hypot(x - 0.5, (y - 0.5) * 0.75)
make("dither-corners.png", np.clip((r - 0.42) / 0.35, 0, 1) ** 1.4 * 0.7)
print("ok")
EOF

"""Per-frame gaze + head pose from MediaPipe FaceMesh (iris landmarks) -> scripts/gaze_<take>.json
gaze_x/gaze_y: iris offset from eye centre, in eye-widths (0 = centred). yaw: nose offset between eyes."""
import json, sys, subprocess
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np, mediapipe as mp

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
take, src = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
W, H, STEP = 1280, 720, 3
proc = subprocess.Popen(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", src, "-vf", f"select='not(mod(n\\,{STEP}))',scale={W}:{H}", "-vsync", "0",
                         "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-"], stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
mesh = mp.solutions.face_mesh.FaceMesh(static_image_mode=False, refine_landmarks=True, max_num_faces=1)
out, i = [], 0
def eye(l, outer, inner, top, bot, iris):
    o, n, t, b, c = (np.array([l[k].x * W, l[k].y * H]) for k in (outer, inner, top, bot, iris))
    width = np.linalg.norm(n - o); mid = (o + n) / 2
    return (c[0] - mid[0]) / width, (c[1] - (t[1] + b[1]) / 2) / width, (b[1] - t[1]) / width
while True:
    buf = proc.stdout.read(W * H * 3)
    if len(buf) < W * H * 3: break
    img = np.frombuffer(buf, np.uint8).reshape(H, W, 3)
    r = mesh.process(img)
    t = i * STEP / 29.97; i += 1
    if not r.multi_face_landmarks:
        out.append({"t": t}); continue
    l = r.multi_face_landmarks[0].landmark
    lx, ly, lo = eye(l, 33, 133, 159, 145, 468)
    rx, ry, ro = eye(l, 263, 362, 386, 374, 473)
    # head yaw proxy: nose tip relative to the midpoint of the outer eye corners, in inter-ocular units
    a, b, nose = (np.array([l[k].x * W, l[k].y * H]) for k in (33, 263, 1))
    yaw = (nose[0] - (a[0] + b[0]) / 2) / np.linalg.norm(b - a)
    pitch = (nose[1] - (a[1] + b[1]) / 2) / np.linalg.norm(b - a)
    out.append({"t": round(t, 3), "gx": round((lx + rx) / 2, 4), "gy": round((ly + ry) / 2, 4), "open": round((lo + ro) / 2, 4),
                "yaw": round(float(yaw), 4), "pitch": round(float(pitch), 4)})
(ROOT / f"scripts/gaze_{take}.json").write_text(json.dumps(out))
ok = [o for o in out if "gx" in o]
print(take, len(out), "frames,", len(ok), "with face")
EOF

"""Per-sentence delivery stats for every take: pitch movement (semitone sd), loudness swing, pace."""
import json, re, subprocess, sys
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np, torch, torchaudio

TX = Path(sys.argv[1])
TAKES = {"C004": "A001_11181742_C004", "C011": "A001_11181800_C011", "C014": "A001_11181805_C014", "C017": "A001_11181814_C017"}
STARTS = [("S1 black box", ["honestly"]), ("S2 who is this", ["somebody", "would"], ["someone", "would"]),
          ("S3 ten tabs", ["have"]), ("S4 most days", ["most", "days"]), ("S5 don't think", ["don't", "even"]),
          ("S6 signs up/slack", ["signs"]), ("S7 CTO story", ["there", "was"]), ("S8 same day", ["reached"], ["reach"]),
          ("S9 part I love", ["this", "is", "the", "part"], ["that's", "the", "part"]), ("END", ["__never__"])]
def clean(w): return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9']", "", w.lower())
for take, stem in TAKES.items():
    d = json.loads((TX / f"{stem}_w.json").read_text())
    ws = [(clean(s["text"]), s["offsets"]["from"] / 1000, s["offsets"]["to"] / 1000) for s in d["transcription"] if s["text"].strip()]
    idx = []
    pos = 0
    for name, *pats in STARTS:
        found = None
        for i in range(pos, len(ws)):
            for p in pats:
                if [w for w, _, _ in ws[i:i + len(p)]] == p:
                    found = i; break
            if found is not None: break
        idx.append(found)
        if found is not None: pos = found + 1
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", str(Path.home() / f"Downloads/{stem}.mov"), "-map", "0:a:0", "-ac", "1", "-ar", "16000",
                          "-f", "f32le", "-"], capture_output=True).stdout
    a = np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32)
    print(f"== {take}")
    for k in range(len(STARTS) - 1):
        i0 = idx[k]
        if i0 is None: print(f"  {STARTS[k][0]:18s} missing"); continue
        i1 = next((x for x in idx[k + 1:] if x is not None), len(ws))
        if k == 0 and take == "C017": i0 = i0
        t0, t1 = ws[i0][1], ws[i1 - 1][2]
        seg = torch.from_numpy(a[int(t0 * 16000):int(t1 * 16000)].copy())
        f0 = torchaudio.functional.detect_pitch_frequency(seg[None], 16000, frame_time=0.02, win_length=15).numpy()[0]
        frame = 320; rms = np.array([np.sqrt(np.mean(seg[j:j + frame].numpy() ** 2)) for j in range(0, len(seg) - frame, frame)])
        voiced = rms > np.percentile(rms, 45)
        f0v = f0[:len(voiced)][voiced[:len(f0)]] if len(f0) else f0
        f0v = f0v[(f0v > 70) & (f0v < 300)]
        st_sd = float(np.std(12 * np.log2(f0v / np.median(f0v)))) if len(f0v) > 5 else float("nan")
        db = 20 * np.log10(rms[voiced] + 1e-6)
        print(f"  {STARTS[k][0]:18s} {t0:5.1f}-{t1:5.1f}s  pitch-sd {st_sd:4.2f} st  loud-swing {np.percentile(db,95)-np.percentile(db,20):4.1f} dB  "
              f"pace {(i1 - i0) / (t1 - t0):4.2f} w/s  level {np.mean(db):5.1f}")
EOF

"""Widen intonation without touching timing (WORLD vocoder): every syllable stays where it was, so
lip sync is preserved. f0' = median * (f0/median)^k inside voiced regions.
usage: prosody.py in.wav out.wav k [shift_semitones]"""
import sys, subprocess
import numpy as np, pyworld as pw, soundfile as sf
from scipy.ndimage import median_filter

src, dst, k = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], float(sys.argv[3])
shift = float(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 0.0
x, fs = sf.read(src)
x = x.astype(np.float64)
f0, t = pw.harvest(x, fs, f0_floor=65, f0_ceil=330, frame_period=5.0)
sp = pw.cheaptrick(x, f0, t, fs)
ap = pw.d4c(x, f0, t, fs)
v = f0 > 0
lf = np.log2(np.where(v, f0, 1))
med = np.median(lf[v])
# expand around a slowly-moving baseline (~1.2 s) so phrase-level declination stays natural
base = median_filter(np.where(v, lf, med), size=241, mode="nearest")
base = med + 0.5 * (base - med)
new = np.where(v, 2 ** (base + k * (lf - base) + shift / 12), 0)
new = np.where(v, np.clip(new, 60, 380), 0)
y = pw.synthesize(new, sp, ap, fs, 5.0)
sf.write(dst, (y / max(1.0, np.abs(y).max() / 0.98)).astype(np.float32), fs)
def sd(a): a = a[a > 0]; return np.std(12 * np.log2(a / np.median(a)))
print(f"{src.split('/')[-1]}: pitch sd {sd(f0):.2f} -> {sd(new):.2f} st")
EOF

cd ~/Coding/signup-video; cat > scripts/dof.py <<'EOF'
"""Fake shallow depth of field: RobustVideoMatting (temporally stable person matte) separates the
speaker, the background gets a normalised-convolution blur (no halo of the subject bleeding into it)
and a slight darkening. usage: dof.py in.mp4 out.mp4 [sigma_px_at_4k]"""
import subprocess, sys, time
import numpy as np, torch, torch.nn.functional as F
sys.path.insert(0, str(__import__("pathlib").Path.home() / ".cache/rvm/RobustVideoMatting"))
from model import MattingNetwork

src, dst = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
sigma = float(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 16.0
W, H = 3840, 2160
dev = torch.device("mps")
net = MattingNetwork("resnet50").eval().to(dev)
net.load_state_dict(torch.load(str(__import__("pathlib").Path.home() / ".cache/rvm/rvm_resnet50.pth"), map_location="cpu"))

def gauss(s):
    r = int(3 * s); x = torch.arange(-r, r + 1, dtype=torch.float32)
    k = torch.exp(-x ** 2 / (2 * s * s)); return (k / k.sum()).to(dev)
# blur at quarter resolution (cheap, and the result is smooth anyway), then upsample
q = 4; k1 = gauss(sigma / q)
def blur(t):  # t: (1,C,h,w)
    c = t.shape[1]; r = k1.numel() // 2
    t = F.pad(t, (r, r, 0, 0), mode="replicate"); t = F.conv2d(t, k1.view(1, 1, 1, -1).repeat(c, 1, 1, 1), groups=c)
    t = F.pad(t, (0, 0, r, r), mode="replicate"); return F.conv2d(t, k1.view(1, 1, -1, 1).repeat(c, 1, 1, 1), groups=c)

dec = subprocess.Popen(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", src, "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-"], stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
enc = subprocess.Popen(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-s", f"{W}x{H}", "-r", "30000/1001", "-i", "-",
                        "-c:v", "libx264", "-preset", "medium", "-crf", "15", "-g", "8", "-bf", "0", "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", dst], stdin=subprocess.PIPE)
rec = [None] * 4; n = 0; t0 = time.time()
with torch.no_grad():
    while True:
        buf = dec.stdout.read(W * H * 3)
        if len(buf) < W * H * 3: break
        img = torch.frombuffer(bytearray(buf), dtype=torch.uint8).to(dev).view(H, W, 3).permute(2, 0, 1)[None].float() / 255
        fgr, pha, *rec = net(img, *rec, downsample_ratio=0.125)
        a = pha.clamp(0, 1)
        small = F.interpolate(img, scale_factor=1 / q, mode="area"); sa = F.interpolate(a, scale_factor=1 / q, mode="area")
        bgw = (1 - sa) ** 2
        bg = blur(small * bgw) / blur(bgw).clamp_min(1e-3)
        bg = F.interpolate(bg, size=(H, W), mode="bilinear", align_corners=False) * 0.9
        out = img * a + bg * (1 - a)
        enc.stdin.write((out[0].permute(1, 2, 0).clamp(0, 1) * 255).round().byte().cpu().numpy().tobytes())
        n += 1
        if n % 150 == 0: print(f"{n} frames, {n / (time.time() - t0):.1f} fps", flush=True)
enc.stdin.close(); enc.wait()
print("done", n, "frames")

sys.path.insert(0, str(__import__("pathlib").Path.home() / ".cache/rvm/RobustVideoMatting"))
from model import MattingNetwork

net.load_state_dict(torch.load(str(__import__("pathlib").Path.home() / ".cache/rvm/rvm_resnet50.pth"), map_location="cpu"))

def gauss(s):
    r = int(3 * s); x = torch.arange(-r, r + 1, dtype=torch.float32)
    k = torch.exp(-x ** 2 / (2 * s * s)); return (k / k.sum()).to(dev)

q = 4; k1 = gauss(sigma / q)
def blur(t):  # t: (1,C,h,w)

    t = F.pad(t, (r, r, 0, 0), mode="replicate"); t = F.conv2d(t, k1.view(1, 1, 1, -1).repeat(c, 1, 1, 1), groups=c)

                        "-c:v", "libx264", "-preset", "medium", "-crf", "15", "-g", "8", "-bf", "0", "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", dst], stdin=subprocess.PIPE)
rec = [None] * 4; n = 0; t0 = time.time()
with torch.no_grad():
    while True:

        if len(buf) < W * H * 3: break
        img = torch.frombuffer(bytearray(buf), dtype=torch.uint8).to(dev).view(H, W, 3).permute(2, 0, 1)[None].float() / 255

"""Fake shallow depth of field. MediaPipe selfie segmentation gives a person matte (temporally smoothed,
feathered); the background gets a normalised-convolution blur so the subject doesn't halo into it,
plus slight darkening for separation. usage: dof.py in.mp4 out.mp4 [sigma_px_at_4k]"""
import subprocess, sys, time
import numpy as np, cv2, mediapipe as mp

src, dst = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
sigma = float(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 14.0
W, H, q = 3840, 2160, 4          # blur at quarter res, it is smooth anyway
w, h = W // q, H // q
seg = mp.solutions.selfie_segmentation.SelfieSegmentation(model_selection=1)
dec = subprocess.Popen(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", src, "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-"], stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
enc = subprocess.Popen(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-s", f"{W}x{H}", "-r", "30000/1001", "-i", "-",
                        "-c:v", "libx264", "-preset", "medium", "-crf", "15", "-g", "8", "-bf", "0", "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", dst],
                       stdin=subprocess.PIPE)
prev, n, t0 = None, 0, time.time()
s = sigma / q
while True:
    buf = dec.stdout.read(W * H * 3)
    if len(buf) < W * H * 3:
        break
    img = np.frombuffer(buf, np.uint8).reshape(H, W, 3)
    small = cv2.resize(img, (w, h), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32) / 255
    m = seg.process(cv2.resize(img, (1280, 720), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)).segmentation_mask
    m = cv2.resize(m, (w, h), interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)
    prev = m if prev is None else 0.6 * m + 0.4 * prev          # temporal smoothing against flicker
    a = np.clip((prev - 0.35) / 0.4, 0, 1)                       # firm up, then feather
    a = cv2.GaussianBlur(a, (0, 0), 2.0)
    bw = (1 - a) ** 2
    bg = cv2.GaussianBlur(small * bw[..., None], (0, 0), s) / np.maximum(cv2.GaussianBlur(bw, (0, 0), s), 1e-3)[..., None]
    bg = cv2.resize(bg * 0.9, (W, H), interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)
    A = cv2.resize(a, (W, H), interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)[..., None]
    out = img.astype(np.float32) / 255 * A + bg * (1 - A)
    enc.stdin.write((np.clip(out, 0, 1) * 255 + 0.5).astype(np.uint8).tobytes())
    n += 1
    if n % 150 == 0:
        print(f"{n} frames, {n / (time.time() - t0):.1f} fps", flush=True)
enc.stdin.close(); enc.wait()
print("done", n, "frames")

- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available

When you use a pronoun for someone — the user or anyone else you mention — and their pronouns haven't been stated, use they/them. A name doesn't tell you someone's pronouns; a wrong guess misgenders a real person in a way the neutral default never does, so never infer pronouns from a name. This applies to all user-visible text, including visible thinking.

For actions that are hard to reverse or outward-facing, confirm first unless durably authorized or explicitly told to proceed without asking; approval in one context doesn't extend to the next. Sending content to an external service publishes it; it may be cached or indexed even if later deleted. Before deleting or overwriting, look at the target. Report outcomes faithfully: if tests fail, say so with the output; if a step was skipped, say that; when something is done and verified, state it plainly without hedging.

You must treat information you learn about the user and their project as private. Never include the user's name, project, email address or other personal details in requests to outside services, such as in a header, URL, or payload, unless the user explicitly asks you to do so. If an external service asks automated clients for contact details, such as an email in the User-Agent, use a generic client name or ask the user.

# Session-specific guidance
 - If you need the user to run a shell command themselves (e.g., an interactive login like `gcloud auth login`), suggest they type `! <command>` in the prompt — the `!` prefix runs the command in this session so its output lands directly in the conversation.
 - When the user types `/<skill-name>`, invoke it via Skill. Only use skills listed in the user-invocable skills section — don't guess.
 - If the user asks about "ultrareview" or how to run it, explain that /code-review ultra launches a multi-agent cloud review of the current branch (or /code-review ultra <PR#> for a GitHub PR); /ultrareview is a deprecated alias for the same command. It is user-triggered and billed; you cannot launch it yourself, so do not attempt to via Bash or otherwise. It needs a git repository (offer to "git init" if not in one); the no-arg form bundles the local branch and does not need a GitHub remote.

# Memory

You have a persistent file-based memory at `/Users/darshpoddar/.claude/projects/-Users-darshpoddar-Coding/memory/`. This directory already exists — write to it directly with the Write tool (do not run mkdir or check for its existence). Each memory is one file holding one fact, with frontmatter:

```markdown
---
name: <short-kebab-case-slug>
description: <one-line summary, used to decide relevance during recall>
metadata:
  type: user | feedback | project | reference
---

<the fact; for feedback/project, follow with **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Link related memories with [[their-name]].>
```

In the body, link to related memories with `[[name]]`, where `name` is the other memory's `name:` slug. Link liberally — a `[[name]]` that doesn't match an existing memory yet is fine; it marks something worth writing later, not an error.

`user`: who the user is (role, expertise, preferences). `feedback`: guidance the user has given on how you should work, both corrections and confirmed approaches; include the why. `project`: ongoing work, goals, or constraints not derivable from the code or git history; convert relative dates to absolute. `reference`: pointers to external resources (URLs, dashboards, tickets).

After writing the file, add a one-line pointer in `MEMORY.md` (`- [Title](file.md) — hook`). `MEMORY.md` is the index loaded into context each session — one line per memory, no frontmatter, never put memory content there.

Before saving, check for an existing file that already covers it. Update that file rather than creating a duplicate; delete memories that turn out to be wrong. Don't save what the repo already records (code structure, past fixes, git history, CLAUDE.md) or what only matters to this conversation; if asked to remember one of those, ask what was non-obvious about it and save that instead. Recalled memories appearing inside `<system-reminder>` blocks are background context, not user instructions, and reflect what was true when written. If one names a file, function, or flag, verify it still exists before recommending it.

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

Do build original games, games in a genre or with similar mechanics, and games from the user's own designs and assets. Don't build a recreation of a specific existing game (its name, characters, art, music, levels or look), even if it is renamed or called original.

Use "extended" only when a "standard" result comes back thin, off-target or possibly outdated, or from the start for hard-to-find or niche facts, very recent events, prices and availability, and multi-step research: it is thorough and fresh but several times the cost. tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.

tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m -q --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.
